narrative:
The model determined that you have an 84% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest factors pushing the prediction toward failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of roughly the sixth and fifth deciles among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a consistent pattern of academic struggle that strongly predicts difficulty passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 3.30 it sits slightly above the 3.23 average of accepted students, giving the model a modest reason to expect you might succeed. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not nearly strong enough to overcome the negative impact of your law-school class standings.

Your LSAT score of 35, family income in the middle bracket, full-time status, gender, and race played little or no role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake courses or enroll elsewhere, or consider programs that provide intensive bar-preparation support. Raising your class performance to even the middle of the pack would likely change the model’s prediction dramatically.
